raw_findings.message: The flush token is embedded in the source, so anyone who can reach the loopback endpoint and inspect the code can authenticate and erase all stored state.
The counter is read and written under separate lock acquisitions, so concurrent increments of the same key can both use the same old value and lose an update.
Adding a client-controlled delta can overflow `i32`, causing a panic in debug builds or a wrapped counter value in release builds.
Each request can add a distinct, unbounded-length counter key that remains in memory, allowing local clients to exhaust server memory with repeated `/incr/` requests.
Prefix matching slices keys at a byte offset that may split a UTF-8 character, so a stored key beginning with a multibyte character and a short prefix can panic the request thread.
The unauthenticated snapshot destination is joined without containment checks, so a path such as `../../target` or an absolute path can make the server overwrite files outside its data directory.
The server reads until a header terminator without a size limit, so a client can send an indefinitely large header and consume memory.
A request line with fewer than two whitespace-separated fields makes the indexed accesses panic, which can be triggered by sending a malformed request.
An arbitrary `Content-Length` is used to allocate the request body before validation, so a client can request an enormous allocation and exhaust server memory.
Malformed percent escapes followed by multibyte UTF-8 can make this byte-indexed string slice split a character and panic the request thread.
The decoded `key` query parameter is interpolated into an HTML response without escaping, so a request containing markup can execute script in a browser.
A thread is spawned for every connection, and clients can keep those threads blocked in request reads indefinitely, allowing local clients to exhaust server resources.

raw_findings.message: The admin token is a fixed credential embedded in the program, so any client that can reach the service and knows the source can use it to flush all stored state.
Keys longer than 32 bytes are silently truncated, so distinct requested keys with the same first 32 bytes alias and overwrite or retrieve the same stored value.
The counter is read and its mutex released before the updated value is written, so concurrent increments can read the same value and overwrite one another.
Adding an attacker-supplied delta to the current counter can overflow i32, causing a panic in overflow-checked builds or a wrapped counter value in other builds.
Prefix matching slices a key at the prefix's byte length without checking for a character boundary, so querying a one-byte prefix against a multibyte key such as `é` panics and poisons the KV mutex.
The snapshot destination is joined without constraining it to the data directory, so a caller can use `../` or an absolute path to overwrite any file writable by the server.
Header bytes are appended to `raw` until a delimiter arrives with no size limit, so a client can consume unbounded memory by sending an excessively large or unterminated header.
A request line with fewer than two whitespace-separated fields panics on indexing `parts`, so malformed input crashes that connection's handler instead of being rejected.
An attacker-controlled Content-Length is used to allocate the entire request body without a limit, allowing a request to exhaust the server's memory.
The percent-decoder slices by byte offsets that may not be UTF-8 character boundaries, so a target such as one containing `%aé` panics the handler.
The query-controlled key is inserted into HTML without escaping, so a crafted `/ui?key=` request can inject script that executes when a victim views the page.
Every accepted connection gets a new thread with no concurrency limit, so many connections that send no data can exhaust the server's threads.

raw_findings.message: The admin flush token is embedded in the source, so anyone who can inspect the code can authenticate to the destructive flush endpoint on the local service.
Counter arithmetic can exceed the i32 range when clients submit large deltas or increment an already large counter, causing a panic in checked builds or a wrapped counter in unchecked builds.
The counter is read and updated under separate lock acquisitions, so concurrent increments of the same key can overwrite one another and lose updates.
A prefix length that falls inside a stored key's multibyte UTF-8 character makes this string slice panic while the map lock is held, poisoning the map and breaking later key operations.
The unauthenticated snapshot destination is joined without restricting absolute paths or `..`, allowing a request to overwrite files outside the data directory wherever the process has write access.
The header-reading loop buffers bytes without a size limit until it sees the terminator, so a client can send an arbitrarily large unterminated header and exhaust memory.
A request line with no tokens, or only one token, indexes outside `parts` and panics instead of rejecting the malformed request.
An attacker-controlled Content-Length is used to allocate the request body without a limit, allowing a single request to trigger excessive allocation or process failure.
Percent-decoding slices the UTF-8 string at byte offsets, so a target such as one containing `%aé` can make the slice end inside a multibyte character and panic.
The `/ui` endpoint inserts the attacker-controlled `key` query parameter into HTML without escaping, allowing a crafted link to execute script in a visitor's browser.
The server spawns an unbounded thread for every connection, and clients can keep those threads occupied by opening connections without completing request headers until resources are exhausted.
